questions.question: Under snapshot isolation, which kind of dependency can exist between two transactions that ran concurrently?
options: Write-write: the second overwrote the first's version
Write-read: the second read the first's committed version
Read-write: one read a version the other then overwrote
None; concurrent transactions are fully independent
questions.explanation: First-committer-wins forbids concurrent write-write, and snapshots hide concurrent writes so write-read cannot happen either. Only read-write antidependencies survive: one transaction read the old version while the other was making a new one. That is why SSI tracks exactly that edge.

questions.question: What is the dangerous structure that SSI aborts on?
options: Any transaction whose read was overwritten by a concurrent writer
A transaction with an incoming and an outgoing rw-edge to concurrent transactions
Two transactions that write the same key within one snapshot window
A cycle of write-read dependencies among three or more transactions
questions.explanation: Fekete et al. proved every non-serializable SI history contains a pivot with T_in -rw-> T_pivot -rw-> T_out. A single overwritten read is one edge and is harmless; aborting on it would be plain optimistic concurrency control with far more aborts. Same-key writes are handled by first-committer-wins, not SSI.

questions.question: Why must a SIREAD lock be kept after its transaction commits?
options: So that vacuum knows which versions the committed transaction still needs
Because a concurrent transaction that began before the commit may still write the key, creating a real rw-edge
So that the next transaction from the same session inherits its snapshot
Because the lock is converted into a shared lock that blocks writers until released
questions.explanation: If R read k and committed, and T began before R committed, T writing k means R saw the old k while T made a new one: R -rw-> T, and R could be the T_in of a dangerous structure. SIREADs never block anything and have nothing to do with vacuum or session state; they are retained until no concurrent transaction remains.

questions.question: In the write-skew history, T2 and T3 each read A and B, T2 writes A, T3 writes B, and T2 commits first. What happens?
options: Both abort, because each is a pivot at the time it commits
T2 aborts as the pivot; its edges are removed and T3 commits
T2 commits and T3 aborts at its own commit with a write conflict
Both commit, because their write sets are disjoint
questions.explanation: T2 has in={T3} and out={T3} when it tries to commit, so it is aborted as a pivot. Aborting removes T2 from T3's conflict sets, leaving T3 with no edges, so T3 commits. Under plain SI both would commit (disjoint write sets); the paper's boolean flags would abort both, which is why the sets are tracked by transaction id.

questions.question: P reads A, writes B, and commits. Q, which started before P committed, reads B and then writes A. When is Q aborted and why?
options: At Q's commit, when its own in and out sets are both non-empty
Never: P already committed, so P cannot be part of a dangerous structure
On Q's write of A, because P is now a committed pivot and Q is the only transaction left to abort
On Q's read of B, because reading a version newer than the snapshot is a serialization failure
questions.explanation: Q's read of B records Q -rw-> P (one edge; P has no out-edge yet, so nothing fires). Q's write of A finds P's retained SIREAD on A and records P -rw-> Q, giving the committed P both edges. P cannot be aborted, so the store aborts Q immediately rather than letting it finish and fail at commit.

questions.question: A ledger service moves to PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE. Which obligation does that place on the application code?
options: Add SELECT ... FOR UPDATE to every read so that SIREAD locks are taken
Wrap every transaction in a retry loop that re-runs it with fresh reads on SQLSTATE 40001
Disable autovacuum during business hours so retained locks are not reclaimed early
Mark every reporting query READ UNCOMMITTED so it cannot become a pivot
questions.explanation: SSI can abort a transaction that did nothing wrong (a false positive) as well as a real pivot, and the only correct response is to retry the whole transaction with new reads. FOR UPDATE is a different, blocking mechanism; vacuum is unrelated to SIREAD retention; and PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, which does not remove the obligation for writers.
